```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(pdmS7)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  error = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 3.6, dpi = if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"))) 110 else 60
)
pal <- c("#444444", "#236b83", "#a26421", "#5b8c3a", "#8a3b6b", "#b23b3b", "#9aa7b0")
```

A rainfall-runoff model is never exactly right, and its errors are not random from one time
step to the next. If the model is 2 m3/s low now, it will very probably be about 2 m3/s low in
15 minutes' time too. **Error correction** uses that. At the moment a forecast is issued, the
latest error is known, because the river has been measured. An autoregressive (AR) model
predicts how that error will carry on, and the forecast becomes the simulation plus the
predicted error.

This is what IMFS does operationally, as post-processing on top of the model. This article
explains, in plain terms, what the AR coefficients mean, where they come from, and where the
method stops working. [Testing forecasts with hindcasts](hindcasts.html) shows how to measure
whether it helps on your catchment.

# Why errors persist

A made-up catchment at 15-minute steps, with a model whose rainfall factor is 10 per cent low
and whose stores are a little too fast:

```{r example}
set.seed(5)
n <- 4 * 24 * 60
wet <- stats::runif(n / 16) < 0.12
rain <- rep(ifelse(wet, stats::rgamma(n / 16, 0.8, scale = 2.5), 0), each = 16) / 4
forcing <- data.frame(rain = rain, pet = 0.01)
truth <- pdm_model(area_km2 = 60, fc = 1.1, dt = 0.25,
                   surface = FlodeCascadeRouting(k1 = 3, k2 = 5))
model <- pdm_model(area_km2 = 60, fc = 1.0, dt = 0.25,
                   surface = FlodeCascadeRouting(k1 = 2, k2 = 4))
observed <- run_pdm(truth, forcing, initial_state_from_flow(truth, 1, 0.7))$output$q_m3s *
  exp(stats::rnorm(n, 0, 0.01))
simulated <- run_pdm(model, forcing, initial_state_from_flow(model, 1, 0.7))$output$q_m3s
error <- observed - simulated
```

The **error** is observed minus simulated, so a positive error means the model is too low.
This is the convention of IMFS and reach.postproc.

```{r error-plot, fig.cap="Top: observed (points) and simulated (line) flow over ten days. Bottom: the error."}
days <- (n - 4 * 24 * 10 + 1):n
hours <- (days - days[1]) / 4
par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(2, 4.2, 0.6, 0.6))
plot(hours, observed[days], pch = 16, cex = 0.2, col = pal[1], xlab = "", ylab = "Flow (m3/s)")
lines(hours, simulated[days], col = pal[2], lwd = 1.5)
par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 0.6, 0.6))
plot(hours, error[days], type = "l", col = pal[3], lwd = 1.5, xlab = "Hours",
     ylab = "Error (m3/s)")
abline(h = 0, col = pal[7], lty = 2)
```

```{r acf, include=FALSE}
lag_cor <- function(k) stats::cor(error[-(1:k)], error[seq_len(n - k)])
```

The error moves slowly: it builds up during a flood and drains away afterwards. Measured over
the whole record, the error now and the error 15 minutes later have a correlation of
`r sprintf("%.3f", lag_cor(1))`; one hour apart, `r sprintf("%.3f", lag_cor(4))`; six hours
apart, still `r sprintf("%.2f", lag_cor(24))`. That memory is what an AR model exploits.

# The simplest case: one coefficient

An AR(1) model says the next error is a fixed fraction of the current one:

> next error = a × current error

With a = 0.9, an error of 1 m3/s is predicted to be 0.9 after one step, 0.81 after two, and so
on: it fades away, more slowly the closer a is to 1. With a = 1 it would never fade, which is
the same as assuming the model stays exactly as wrong as it is now.

```{r ar1-plot, fig.height=3.2, fig.cap="How an error of 1 m3/s is carried forward by AR(1) models, at 15-minute steps."}
project <- function(a, start, steps) {
  e <- start
  out <- numeric(steps)
  for (k in seq_len(steps)) {
    out[k] <- sum(a * e)
    e <- c(out[k], e[-length(e)])
  }
  out
}
steps <- 4 * 48
lead <- seq_len(steps) / 4
par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 0.6, 0.6))
plot(range(lead), c(0, 1), type = "n", xlab = "Lead time (h)", ylab = "Predicted error (m3/s)")
for (i in 1:3) {
  a <- c(0.9, 0.98, 0.995)[i]
  lines(lead, project(a, 1, steps), col = pal[i + 1], lwd = 2)
}
legend("topright", paste("a =", c(0.9, 0.98, 0.995)), col = pal[2:4], lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

The time an error takes to fall to 37 per cent (1/e) of its size is its **decay time**:
-1 / log(a) steps. For a = 0.98 that is `r round(-1 / log(0.98))` steps, about
`r round(-1 / log(0.98) / 4)` hours at 15 minutes.

# Three coefficients: the IMFS models

IMFS uses three coefficients, AR(3): the next error depends on the last three.

> next error = a1 × current error + a2 × previous error + a3 × the one before

Three past values carry more than size. They also carry direction: whether the error is
growing or shrinking. The Environment Agency 2024 default set is

```{r ea}
ar_ea_default()
```

These numbers are hard to read directly, because they work together. Two views help.

## What it does to a steady error, and to a growing one

```{r ea-plot, fig.cap="The EA 2024 default projecting an error that has been steady at 1 m3/s, and one that has been growing (0.6, 0.8, then 1 m3/s)."}
ea <- ar_ea_default()
steady <- project(ea, c(1, 1, 1), steps)
growing <- project(ea, c(1, 0.8, 0.6), steps)
par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 0.6, 0.6))
plot(range(lead), range(c(0, steady, growing)), type = "n", xlab = "Lead time (h)",
     ylab = "Predicted error (m3/s)")
lines(lead, steady, col = pal[2], lwd = 2)
lines(lead, growing, col = pal[3], lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("steady error", "growing error"), col = pal[2:3], lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

```{r ea-numbers, include=FALSE}
at_h <- function(x, h) sprintf("%.2f", x[h * 4])
peak_h <- which.max(growing) / 4
```

A steady error of 1 m3/s fades slowly: `r at_h(steady, 6)` after 6 hours,
`r at_h(steady, 24)` after a day. A growing error **keeps growing** for a while, to a peak of
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(growing))` m3/s about `r round(peak_h, 1)` hours ahead, before it too
fades. The model extrapolates the recent trend in the error. On a rising limb where the model
is falling further behind, that is exactly right. Where the error was growing because of gauge
noise or a short blip, the AR model projects the blip forward. That is why
[the hindcast](hindcasts.html) found it no better than persistence in the first hour on noisy
data.

## Roots: the timescales inside the model

An AR(3) model behaves like three simple fading processes added together, one for each
**root** of its characteristic equation. Each root has its own decay time, and that splits the
coefficients into timescales a hydrologist can read:

```{r roots}
ar_roots <- function(a) {
  z <- polyroot(c(-rev(unname(a)), 1))
  data.frame(root = format(round(z, 4)), decay_steps = round(-1 / log(Mod(z)), 2),
             decay_hours_at_15min = round(-1 / log(Mod(z)) / 4, 2))
}
ar_roots(ea)
```

The EA default has:

- a **slow root**, near 1, decaying over about a day: the persistence of the error;
- a **medium root**, decaying in about five steps: this one carries the trend;
- a **tiny negative root**, gone within a step: it only fine-tunes the first step.

The model is **stable** if every root lies strictly between -1 and 1 in size. A root of size 1
or more would make a projected error grow without limit. `reach.postproc::assess()` applies the
Environment Agency's review criteria to a parameter set, including stability, decay times that
are too long or too short, and unwanted oscillation. Use it on any set before operational use.

# Where coefficients come from

| Source | Function | When |
|---|---|---|
| EA 2024 default | `ar_ea_default()` | No better information; defined for 15-minute steps |
| The default family, from one timescale | `ar_from_response_time()` | You know how fast the catchment responds |
| Fitted to this model's errors | `fit_error_updater()`, or `fit_window` in `pdm_hindcast()` | A long record of this model's errors exists |
| Fitted to flood events only | `reach.postproc::fit_ar_from_events()` | Floods are what matter, and there are enough of them |

## The default family

The EA default is one member of a family of AR(3) sets, all sharing the same first
coefficient and fast root, and differing only in the decay time of the slow root.
`ar_from_response_time()` builds a member from one timescale, by the same construction as
`reach.postproc::default_family_ar_parameters()`. pdmS7 offers the model's own time to peak
from `pdm_response_time()` as that timescale.

```{r family-plot, fig.cap="A steady error projected by members of the default family, labelled by their principal decay time, at 15-minute steps."}
decays <- c(3, 12, 24, 96)
par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 0.6, 0.6))
plot(range(lead), c(0, 1), type = "n", xlab = "Lead time (h)",
     ylab = "Predicted error (m3/s)")
for (i in seq_along(decays)) {
  lines(lead, project(ar_from_response_time(decays[i], dt = 0.25), c(1, 1, 1), steps),
        col = pal[i + 1], lwd = 2)
}
legend("topright", paste(decays, "h"), col = pal[2:5], lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

The EA 2024 default sits almost exactly on the 24-hour member. A flashy catchment, with a short
time to peak, gets a correction that fades quickly; a slow one keeps its correction for longer.
Linking the forecast error's decay to the catchment's time to peak is an approximation, the
same one reach.postproc makes, so check the result with a hindcast.

## Fitting

`fit_error_updater()` fits the coefficients to a model's errors by maximum likelihood, using
`stats::arima()`:

```{r fit}
calibration <- seq_len(n / 2)
fitted <- fit_error_updater(observed[calibration], simulated[calibration], order = c(3, 0))
round(fitted$updater@ar, 4)
ar_roots(fitted$updater@ar)
```

```{r fit-numbers, include=FALSE}
fit_roots <- polyroot(c(-rev(unname(fitted$updater@ar)), 1))
slowest_h <- max(-1 / log(Mod(fit_roots))) / 4
oscillates <- any(abs(Im(fit_roots)) > 1e-8)
```

The fitted set is quite unlike the default. Its slowest root decays over about
`r round(slowest_h)` hours, against the default's 24`r if (oscillates) ", and its two fast roots are a complex pair, which makes the projected error wobble from step to step"`.
A long decay time is the fit's way of saying this model's error is mostly a persistent bias,
the low rainfall factor, which is true here. `reach.postproc::assess()` would test both the
decay time and any oscillation against the review criteria.

A fit reflects this model's errors, in this catchment, over this period. It changes whenever
the model is recalibrated. A fit over a whole record is weighted towards quiet weather, because
there is more of it, and gauge noise pulls the coefficients towards fast decay. Fitting to
flood events only, as `reach.postproc::fit_ar_from_events()` does, targets the conditions that
matter. Whichever you use, judge it on events it was not fitted to.

# Sign conventions

The same model can be written with opposite signs, and mixing them up turns a stable model
into an unstable one. pdmS7 follows IMFS, Deltares and reach.postproc:

| Convention | Written as | EA 2024 default |
|---|---|---|
| Deltares, IMFS, reach.postproc, pdmS7 | next error = a1 × current + a2 × previous + a3 × earlier | a = 1.765, -0.72625, -0.040656 |
| Moore (2007), equation 31 | coefficients phi = -a | phi = -1.765, 0.72625, 0.040656 |

`error_updater(ar = )` takes the Deltares values, so a set can be copied from IMFS or
reach.postproc unchanged.

# ARMA: adding a moving average

An ARMA model adds **moving-average** (MA) terms: the next error also depends on recent
*surprises*, the parts of recent errors the AR terms did not predict. They let the model react
to a sudden change, such as a shift in the rating, without the long memory of the AR part.
pdmS7 supports them, with `error_updater(ar = , ma = )` and
`fit_error_updater(order = c(p, q))`, and Moore (2007) describes them, but IMFS uses AR only.
Start with AR(3); add an MA term only if a hindcast shows it helps.

```{r arma}
arma <- fit_error_updater(observed[calibration], simulated[calibration], order = c(2, 1))
c(ar = round(arma$updater@ar, 3), ma = round(arma$updater@ma, 3))
```

# Additive or log errors

By default errors are in m3/s, **additive**, as in IMFS. With `scale = "log"` they are taken
on the log scale, so a 10 per cent error at high flow counts the same as a 10 per cent error at
low flow, and a correction can never make the flow negative. Additive correction can push a low
flow below zero; `pdm_hindcast()` raises any updated flow below `lower_limit`, 0 by default,
back up to it.

# Where AR correction stops working

AR correction predicts how the error develops. It does not know about the river. So:

- **Timing errors.** If the model's flood arrives an hour late, the error swings positive then
  negative. The AR model sees only the first half and projects it forward, the wrong way.
- **Noise.** Gauge noise in the latest observation is projected forward as if it were real.
- **Gaps.** With a missing observation in the last three steps, there is no projection; the
  hindcast leaves that origin out.
- **Ratings.** A correction made in flow does not keep its shape when converted to level
  through a nonlinear rating, and the reverse.
- **Beyond the decay time,** the correction has faded and the forecast is the model's alone.

The way to know whether it helps, and at which lead times, is to test it on past events:
[Testing forecasts with hindcasts](hindcasts.html).

# Summary

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What is corrected? | The error, observed minus simulated, projected forward from the forecast origin |
| What do the coefficients mean? | Read them through their roots: each root is a decay time |
| Which set? | Start from the EA 2024 default or `ar_from_response_time()`; fit only with care |
| Is it stable? | Every root smaller than 1 in size; check with `reach.postproc::assess()` |
| Does it help here? | Run `pdm_hindcast()` and compare skill against persistence by lead time |
